title: "The export sheet"
description: "Choose a format and its settings, see what the file will be before anything is written, then export now or add the job to the queue."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

One sheet turns the timeline into a movie, an audio file or an animated image. It shows you the size, rate, length and codec of the file before anything is written.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="The accent Export… button at the right end of the toolbar"
  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
/>

## Open the export sheet

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Export…**, press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, or click **Export…** at the right end of the toolbar. Playback pauses and the sheet opens over the editor window.

2. Choose a [format](/export/formats/), then change whichever other controls you need.

3. Read the [readout line](#the-readout-line) and the [footnote](#the-footnote) under the controls. They say what the file will be.

4. Choose [**Export…** or **Add to Queue**](#export-or-add-to-queue), then pick where to save the file.

</Steps>

While the timeline is empty, **File ▸ Export…** is greyed out and there's no sheet to open. A timeline of nothing but text, shapes, images and graphics still exports. You can't edit the project while the sheet is open.

An export always writes the whole timeline, even when you're working inside a [nest](/editing/nests/).

<Shot
  name="12-export-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Export sheet with a paragraph of help under its title, then the controls: Preset on Custom, Format on H.264 (MP4), Speed greyed on Balanced, Size on Document size 960 × 540 with two greyed fields, Frame rate on Project rate, Quality on Format default, Bit depth greyed on 16-bit, Stems greyed on None, Loudness on Off, Range greyed on Whole project, and an unticked Burn in timecode. Below
/>

## The controls

The paragraph under the sheet's title sums up the main rules. The controls run from top to bottom:

| Control | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Preset:** | Applies a set of choices you saved. The gear beside it saves and deletes them. See [Export presets](/export/presets/). | Custom |
| **Format:** | The encoding, a container and a codec together. See [Choose a format](/export/formats/). | H.264 (MP4) |
| **Dynamic Range:** | Which picture an HDR project writes. The row is there only in an HDR project. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/). | HDR (HLG) |
| **Speed:** | How long the AV1 encoder works on each frame. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). | Balanced |
| **Size:** | The frame size, or **Custom…** with width and height fields on the row below. See [Export size](/export/size/). | The format's first row |
| **Frame rate:** | **Project rate**, or a fixed rate. See [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/). | Project rate |
| **Quality:** | **Format default**, or a bit-rate tier. See [Export quality](/export/quality/). | Format default |
| **Bit depth:** | **16-bit** or **24-bit**, for a WAV or an AIFF. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). | 16-bit |
| **Stems:** | Also writes each track's sound as its own file. See [Audio stems](/export/stems/). | None |
| **Loudness:** | **Off**, a loudness target, or **Custom…** with a LUFS field. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/). | Off |
| **Range:** | **Whole project**, or **In/out range** when one is set. See [Export a range](/export/range/). | Whole project |
| **Burn in timecode** | Draws the project timecode into the exported picture. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/). | Off |

Every export's sound goes through a master limiter, whatever you choose here. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).

## Unavailable controls

A control the chosen format can't use is greyed out rather than hidden, and its value isn't sent. So a greyed-out control never affects the file.

| Control | Available on |
| --- | --- |
| **Dynamic Range:** | HEVC 10-bit (MP4), AV1 (MP4), AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM), ProRes 422 (MOV) and ProRes 4444 (MOV). On any other format it's greyed out and shows **SDR version**, which is what that format writes. |
| **Speed:** | AV1 (MP4) and AV1 (WebM) |

---
title: Word caption styles
description: Make the large word-by-word captions used in shorts and reels, choose how the spoken word is marked, and see how pages are filled for your canvas.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The five word styles make the large captions used in shorts and reels, where each word is marked as it's said. For classic two-line cues, use [Subtitles](/captions/subtitles/) instead.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Generate Captions…"
  where="The Generate Captions sheet ▸ Style:"
  tools="transcribe"
/>

## Make word captions

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Generate Captions…**.

2. Set **Language:**, **Engine:** and **From:**. [Generate Captions](/captions/generate-captions/) explains each one.

3. Set **Style:** to **Highlight**, **Pill**, **Karaoke**, **Build** or **One Word**. The sheet remembers your choice for next time.

4. Tick any [looks](/captions/word-caption-looks/) you want, and check the [preview](#the-sheets-two-frame-preview).

5. Choose **Generate**.

</Steps>

## Word caption pages

A word style doesn't make cues. Each clip holds a **page** of words, with each word's timing, and the word being spoken is drawn the way the style says. A page is still an ordinary [text clip](/captions/how-captions-work/), so you can drag, trim and split it.

All five styles are white with the spoken word marked. Words are marked by their timing only, so there's no keyword emphasis and no emoji.

The text is 7.5% of the canvas's shorter side, or 12% for One Word. That means a vertical and a horizontal canvas get the same text height: on both 1080 × 1920 and 1920 × 1080 it's 81 px, or 130 px for One Word. Where a style pops the spoken word, the pop takes 0.12 s.

## The five styles

### Highlight

The spoken word turns yellow and pops to 112%, and the other words stay white.

Montserrat Black with a black outline, in capitals. The box is centred a quarter of the frame height below the middle.

### Pill

---
title: "Export captions"
description: "Write a track of captions out as a SubRip or WebVTT file to ship beside your movie, without changing the project."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Export Captions writes one track of captions out as a separate subtitle file, for a platform or player that takes one. Burned-in captions need none of this: they're part of the picture in any [movie you export](/export/export-sheet/).

<AtAGlance menu="File ▸ Export Captions…" tools="export_captions" />

## Export captions

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Export Captions…**. It has no keyboard shortcut, and it's greyed out until some track holds only text clips, with caption text on at least one of them.

2. In the save panel, choose the [**Track**](#track) and the [**Format**](#format-subrip-or-webvtt). The name starts as your project's name with `.srt` on the end.

3. Choose **Save**.

</Steps>

Exporting changes nothing in the project, so there's no undo step. If the file can't be written, an alert says why.

## Track

The **Track** pop-up lists the tracks you can write, front-most first, with the front-most chosen. Each row reads like "Captions — 12 cues (track 4)". The pop-up is greyed when there's only one to choose.

Nothing marks a track as a caption track, so any track made only of text clips is listed, a titles track included. A track with any other kind of clip on it isn't listed, and neither is one whose text clips are all empty.

With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open, the list shows that nest's tracks.

## Format: SubRip or WebVTT

The **Format** pop-up offers **SubRip (.srt)**, the default, and **WebVTT (.vtt)**. Choose whichever your player or platform asks for. Changing it changes the extension in the name field and keeps the name you've typed.

The words and times are the same in both. The files differ like this:

| | SubRip | WebVTT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First line of the file | The first cue | `WEBVTT` |
| A number above each cue | Yes | No |
| Timestamps | `00:00:04,133` | `00:00:04.133` |
| `&`, `<` and `>` in the text | Written as they are | Escaped |

Both use Unix (LF) line endings and end with one newline.

## One cue per text clip
---
title: Remove Silences
description: Find the dead air in a spoken recording, see it on the timeline, and cut it all as one edit.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Remove Silences finds the dead air in a spoken recording, shows you what it would cut, and takes it all out as one undo step, closing the timeline over each cut. Use it on a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Remove Silences…"
  tools={['detect_silence', 'ripple_delete_ranges']}
  needs="Nothing. Voice detection runs on your Mac, with no key and no upload."
/>

## Remove the silences

<Steps>

1. To measure only some clips, select them first. The sheet then opens on **Selected clips**.

2. Choose **Clip ▸ Remove Silences…**. It's available when the timeline has a clip with its sound on. If there turns out to be nothing to measure, Frame Job beeps instead of opening the sheet.

3. Check what's shaded on the timeline, and read the count in the sheet, for example "23 cuts · removes 00:00:04:12". Both update as you change a control. With nothing to cut the count reads "No cuts" and **Remove** is dimmed.

4. Adjust the [controls](#the-controls) until the cuts look right.

5. Choose **Remove**. Everything shaded is cut and the timeline closes up. <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> puts it all back. Choose **Cancel** to leave the timeline as it was.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="14-remove-silences-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Remove Silences sheet, with Judge by set to Voice, a Level if no voice slider at −40 dBFS, Longer than 0.5 seconds, Keep at ends 0.1 seconds, and In set to All audible clips."
/>

The sheet opens on its defaults every time. It doesn't remember your last settings.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Judge by:** | How a moment is tested. See [What counts as silent](/cleanup/voice-or-level/). | Voice, or Level if the voice model can't be used | Voice, Level |
| **Quieter than:** or **Level if no voice:** | The level that counts as quiet. The row reads **Quieter than:** in Level mode and **Level if no voice:** in Voice mode. | −40 dBFS | −80 to −10 dBFS |
| **Longer than:** | The shortest quiet stretch worth cutting. Shorter pauses, such as the gap between two words, stay. | 0.5 s | 0.05 to 10 s |
| **Keep at ends:** | How much of each quiet stretch to keep at each end, so speech doesn't start or stop abruptly. | 0.1 s | 0 to 2 s |
| **In:** | Whether to look at **Selected clips** or **All audible clips**. | Selected clips when the selection has something audible, otherwise All audible clips | |

---
title: "Remove Filler Words"
description: "Find the ums and uhs in your speech, see what would go, and cut them all as one edit."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Remove Filler Words finds the ums and uhs in your speech, shows you what it would cut, and cuts them at the words' own timings, all as one undo step. There's nothing to tune.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…"
  tools={['detect_fillers', 'transcribe_for_fillers', 'ripple_delete_ranges', 'get_transcript', 'get_timeline_transcript']}
  needs="An AssemblyAI key, unless a file it would read already has a transcript made with filler words."
/>

## Remove the filler words

<Steps>

1. If you only want some clips read, select them. See [Which clips are read](#which-clips-are-read).

2. Choose **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…**. It's after **Remove Silences…** and has no keyboard shortcut.

3. If the sheet lists files with no filler transcript yet, press **Transcribe** beside each one you want read. This uploads the file's audio to AssemblyAI and costs money, so the sheet shows the estimate first. See [Transcripts for filler words](/cleanup/filler-transcripts/).

4. Check what's shaded on the timeline, and read the count in the sheet, such as "3 cuts · removes 00:00:01:12".

5. Choose **Remove**, or **Cancel** to leave the timeline as it was. Closing the sheet also stops a transcription that's still running.

</Steps>

**Remove** is off while the sheet reads "No cuts" and while a transcription is running. One <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> puts everything back, because the whole cut is a single **Remove Filler Words** undo step.

The command is available when the timeline has a clip that plays sound from a media file, forwards, with its sound on, and you've either set an AssemblyAI key or a file it would read already has a transcript made with filler words. With neither, it's greyed and reads **Remove Filler Words… (needs your AssemblyAI key)**. See [Your AssemblyAI key](/captions/assemblyai-key/).

## Which words are fillers

A word counts as a filler when it's on this fixed list, ignoring capitals and any punctuation at its ends:

um · uh · hmm · mhm · uh-huh · ah · huh · hm · m · er · erm

"Uh huh" written as two words matches as two fillers, and "uh-huh" matches as one.

:::caution
The list can't be changed, and the sheet can't keep a single filler. A real "ah" or "er", or the letter "M" said aloud, is treated as a filler too, so check the shading before you choose **Remove**.
:::

## Which clips are read

---
title: "Zoom and pan the preview"
description: "Look closer at the picture with the zoom popup, the View menu or a pinch, and move around a canvas bigger than the pane."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Zoom the preview to look closely at the picture or to place something precisely, then pan to reach the part you want. Zooming is only a way of looking: it changes nothing in the project, makes no undo step and is never exported.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['View ▸ Zoom In', 'View ▸ Zoom Out', 'View ▸ Zoom to Fit']}
  keys={['⌘+', '⌘=', '⌘-', '⌘0']}
  where={['The zoom popup in the toolbar', 'Pinch, ⌥-scroll or ⌘-scroll over the preview', 'Scroll or Space-drag to pan']}
/>

## The zoom popup

The popup in the toolbar sets how large the picture appears. Its stops are **Fit**, **50%**, **100%** and **200%**. It always shows the zoom the canvas is at, however you got there.

**Fit** sizes the canvas to the pane and follows the pane as it changes. At **100%**, one canvas pixel takes one point on screen.

Each window starts at **Fit**, and the zoom isn't saved with the project.

## View menu commands

| Command | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **View ▸ Zoom In** | <kbd>⌘+</kbd> or <kbd>⌘=</kbd> | Goes to the next stop up. Greyed at 200%. |
| **View ▸ Zoom Out** | <kbd>⌘-</kbd> | Goes to the next stop down. Greyed at Fit. |
| **View ▸ Zoom to Fit** | <kbd>⌘0</kbd> | Goes straight back to Fit and centres the canvas. Greyed at Fit. |

These zoom the preview. To zoom the timeline, see [Zoom and scroll the timeline](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/).

## Pinch and scroll

Pinch on a trackpad over the preview, or scroll with <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> held, to step through the same four stops. The stops are separate steps, so a gesture has to build up a little before it takes the next one.

## Panning

When the zoomed canvas is bigger than the pane, there are two ways to move it:
---
title: "Zoom to Region"
description: "Draw a rectangle on the picture to zoom a clip to it, then pull back out with Zoom Back."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Zoom to Region is the screencast zoom: draw a rectangle on the picture, and the clip zooms until that rectangle fills the frame. The zoom is an ordinary [action](/motion/actions/), so you can retime it, change its curve or remove it like any other.

<AtAGlance
  keys="Z"
  where={['Clip tab ▸ action lane ▸ zoom-in magnifier (Zoom to Region)', 'Clip tab ▸ action lane ▸ zoom-out magnifier (Zoom Back)']}
  tools="add_zoom_action"
/>

## Draw a zoom

<Steps>

1. Select one clip and put the playhead where the zoom should start.

2. Press <kbd>Z</kbd>, or click the zoom-in magnifier in the [action lane](/motion/action-lane/). The pointer becomes a crosshair and a hint appears on the canvas.

3. Drag a rectangle over the canvas. It can start outside the picture, which helps when you want to catch the edge of the frame.

4. Release the mouse.

</Steps>

Frame Job adds a 1-second **Ease In Out** action at the playhead, shown as **In Out** in the lane's Curve pop-up. Its end state is the scale and position that bring the rectangle to the canvas, allowing for the clip's rotation and crop at that moment. It's one undo step, Zoom to Region.

The new action is selected, so you can go straight on to change its length or curve in the lane's [detail row](/motion/action-lane/#detail-row), or adjust where it ends with the [Clip tab's fields or the canvas](/motion/edit-an-action/).

The clip stays zoomed after the action ends, until a later action changes it. [Zoom Back](#zoom-back) is the way to pull out again.

## The canvas hint and outline

While the mode is on, a hint at the top of the canvas reads "Drag a rectangle to zoom to it · ⇧ fills · Esc to cancel".

As you drag, you see two outlines: the rectangle you're drawing, and a dimmer dashed one showing exactly what the canvas will show once the zoom lands. They differ when your rectangle isn't the shape of the canvas.

## Fit or fill

| To | Do this | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fit | Drag | The whole rectangle is shown. This is the default. |
| Fill | Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> while dragging | The rectangle fills the canvas, and whatever doesn't match the canvas shape is cropped. |

Frame Job reads <kbd>⇧</kbd> at every step of the drag, so you can change your mind before you let go, and the dashed outline follows.
---
title: "Auto Zoom"
description: "Zoom a screen recording in where things happen, planned from its cursor file, with every zoom left as an ordinary action you can change."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Auto Zoom moves a screen recording in where things happen. It reads the recording's [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/), arrives at each click as it happens, stays while you keep working there, and zooms back out once you stop, so a viewer can see what you clicked without you zooming each moment

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…"
  where="Zoom in on clicks, under When it lands: in the recorder panel"
  tools="auto_zoom"
  needs="A recording with a cursor file. Nothing else: it plans from that file on your Mac, with no picture analysis and no key."
/>

## Zoom a recording

<Steps>

1. Select one or more clips of a screen recording. **Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…** is available when every selected clip is a movie with a cursor file, and no sheet is up. It works inside an open [nest](/editing/nests/) too.

2. Choose **Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…**. The sheet reads "Reading cursor files…" and **Zoom** is dimmed until they're read and there's a plan.

3. Adjust the [controls](#the-controls). The line under them [says what you'd get](#what-the-sheet-tells-you).

4. Choose **Zoom**, or **Cancel** to leave the timeline as it was.

</Steps>

The whole plan is one undo step, **Auto Zoom**.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Zoom:** | How far in, as a multiple of the clip's own size. | 2× | 1.25 to 4× |
| **Arrive:** | How long the zoom takes, in seconds. It starts this long before the click and is fully in on the click. | 0.6 s | 0.2 to 2 s |
| **Stay:** | How long the zoom holds after the last click or typing before it starts back out. | 2.5 s | 0.5 to 10 s |
| **Follow the cursor while zoomed** | Pans along when the pointer stays near the edge of the zoomed view. | On | |
| **Zoom on typing** | Zooms in on stretches of typing as well as clicks. | On when the recording holds typing | |
| **Replace existing zooms** | Removes the clips' existing zooms first. | Off | |
| **Motion blur** | Gives each zoomed clip a 50 % motion blur. | On | |

The number fields take up to two decimal places, and each value is held to its range.

### Follow the cursor while zoomed

When the pointer stays outside the middle 70 % of the zoomed view for 0.3 s, the view makes a half-second pan to it. It makes at most one of these pans a second, and none that would run into the zoom back out or a pan to a coming click.
---
title: "The cursor in a recording"
description: "Choose whether the pointer is kept out of a screen recording for Frame Job to draw, or drawn into the movie by macOS, and how clicks are shown."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A screen recording can keep the pointer out of the movie, so Frame Job draws it on the clip and you can restyle it later, or have macOS draw it into the picture for good. You choose before you record, because the choice is part of the movie.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ New Recording…"
  keys="⌥⌘N"
  where={['New Recording panel ▸ Cursor', 'New Recording panel ▸ Show Clicks']}
  tools="record_screen"
/>

## Choose Separate or In the picture

Set **Cursor** on the [recorder panel](/recording/recorder-panel/).

| | **Separate** | **In the picture** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The pointer | Kept out of the movie. Frame Job draws it on the clip. | Drawn into the movie by macOS. |
| Restyle it later | Yes, in the clip's **Cursor** section. | No. It can't be changed or removed. |
| **Show Clicks** | Click ripples, drawn by Frame Job. | A ring drawn into the movie. |
| The **Cursor** section | Appears on the clip. | Doesn't appear. |
| Cursor file | Written | Written |

**Separate** is the default for every screen source: displays, windows and picked windows. Your choice is remembered, and once you've made one it holds for every source.

Both write a [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/) beside the movie, so [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/), [shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) and [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) work either way.

With **Separate**, the pointer appears wherever Frame Job draws the clip, in the preview and in every export. The movie file on its own has no pointer, so opened in another app it shows none.

**Cursor** is greyed out, keeping its value, with **Camera** or **Microphone Only** as the source, and while a recording is under way.

## Show clicks

**Show Clicks** marks each mouse click. It's off by default, and greyed out with **Camera** or **Microphone Only**.

- **With In the picture**, macOS draws a ring around each click into the movie. It can't be removed afterwards.
- **With Separate**, nothing is drawn into the movie. Frame Job draws the ripples from the cursor file, and you can edit them afterwards.

## What a Separate recording lands with

The clip gets a **Cursor** section on the Clip tab's **Picture** sub-tab, with the pointer drawn as recorded. See [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/) for what you can change there.

With **Show Clicks** on as well, the clips land with **Clicks** set to **Ripple**, in the same undo step as the recording. In a new project where that's the only other change, the undo step is called **Cursor Clicks**. Undoing it takes the ripples off and keeps the pointer.

Nothing else is set. To smooth the pointer's path and hide it when it's idle, choose **Polish** in the same section.

## What an In the picture recording lands with

The pointer is in the movie and the cursor file says so, so the clip shows no **Cursor** section and nothing is drawn twice.

## Good to know

If a **Separate** stretch's cursor file couldn't be written, that stretch has no pointer at all: it isn't in the movie and there's nothing to draw it from. It gets no ripples either. The panel's note says so, with "The pointer is not in the movie either: it was recorded Separate."

## With an agent

`record_screen` takes `cursor`, either `separate` or `in_picture`, and leaving it out means `separate`. Its `show_clicks` is `false` unless the agent sets it. Neither can be used with a voice-over or a camera on its own. See [Record with record_screen](/mcp/record-screen/#pointer-and-keys).

## Related

- [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/)
- [Cursor files](/recording/cursor-files/)
- [The recorder panel](/recording/recorder-panel/)
- [Record with record_screen](/mcp/record-screen/)

---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

When a screen recording keeps its pointer out of the movie, Frame Job draws the pointer for you, so you can restyle it long after you stopped recording. The **Cursor** section makes it bigger, calms a shaky path, hides it when it rests and puts a ring on every click.

<AtAGlance
  where="Clip tab ▸ Picture ▸ Cursor"
  tools={['set_video', 'paste_attributes', 'get_cursor_events']}
  needs="A screen recording made with Cursor set to Separate, the default, so its pointer isn't in the movie."
/>

## Find the Cursor section

<Steps>

1. Select a recording's clip on the timeline.

2. Open the **Clip** tab's **Picture** sub-tab.

3. Open the **Cursor** section, after **Background**. It starts shut.

</Steps>

The section's header sums up what's set: **off**, **on** or **arrow**, with **+ ripples** when clicks ripple.

The section is there only when every selected clip comes from a movie with a [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/) that the picture doesn't already show:

- A recording made with **Cursor:** set to **In the picture** has no section, because the pointer is part of the movie and would otherwise be drawn twice. See [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/).
- A movie with no cursor file has no section. If the file exists but didn't come along, [attach it with Locate…](/recording/cursor-files/#attach-or-re-point-a-cursor-file).
- A selection that also holds any other kind of clip has no section.

A freeze frame of a recording has the section too, with the pointer held where it was on that frame.

Each row is its own undo step. If the selected clips disagree about a row, it shows as mixed.

## Tidy the pointer in one click

Choose **Polish** at the bottom of the section. It sets **Smoothing** to **Medium** and **Hide when idle** to **3 s**, as one undo step called "Polish Cursor". Nothing else changes, and you can adjust either row afterwards.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Show cursor** | Draws the pointer. | On | On, off |
| **Size** | How big the pointer is drawn. | 100 % | 25–800 % |
| **Style** | Which pointer is drawn. | As recorded | As recorded, Arrow |
| **Smoothing** | Calms a shaky path. | Off | Off, Light, Medium, Strong |
| **Hide when idle** | Fades out a resting pointer. | Never | Never, 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 s |
| **Clicks** | Draws a ring out of every click. | None | None, Ripple |
| **Ripple color** | The ring's colour, with opacity. | White at 80 % | Any colour |
| **Ripple size** | How big the ring grows. | 100 % | 25–400 % |

## Show or resize the pointer

Untick **Show cursor** to draw no pointer on this clip. Click rings are separate, so with **Clicks** set to **Ripple** the rings still draw without a pointer. That's useful when you want to show where someone clicked and nothing else.

title: "Shortcut overlays"

---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Shortcut overlays show a viewer what you pressed. Each keyboard shortcut in a screen recording appears as keycaps on screen at the moment you pressed it, so nobody has to guess how you did that.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Add Shortcut Overlays"
  where="Show shortcuts, under When it lands: in the recorder panel"
  tools="add_shortcut_overlays"
  needs="A recording made with Record shortcuts on, which needs macOS's Input Monitoring permission. No key: it runs on your Mac."
/>

## Add the overlays

<Steps>

1. Make the recording with [Record shortcuts](/recording/record-shortcuts/) on. It records your shortcuts and when you type, never what you typed.

2. Select one or more clips of the recording. The menu item is available when every selected clip is a movie with a [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/) and no sheet is up. It works inside an open [nest](/editing/nests/) too.

3. Choose **Clip ▸ Add Shortcut Overlays**.

</Steps>

There's no sheet. Frame Job reads the cursor files, with the item dimmed while it does, and places one **Keyboard keys** graphic clip per shortcut on a [Shortcuts track](#the-shortcuts-track). Each sits at the bottom of the picture in the dark theme and shows for 1.5 s.

The whole change is one undo step, **Add Shortcut Overlays**. If some shortcuts couldn't be shown, or nothing could be added, a [sheet says so](#what-the-sheet-tells-you).

## What an overlay shows

The keycaps pop in one after another, each is pressed in turn, and the group fades out at the end of the clip. ⌘, ⇧, ⌥, ⌃ and the arrow keys are drawn as symbols, a single character as its capital, and a named key such as `return` or `f5` as its word.

## How overlays are timed

**Where it starts.** An overlay starts on the frame where the press plays, following the clip's speed and any speed ramp. Only the part of a clip that plays counts, so a shortcut in a part you've trimmed away gets no overlay.

title: Ducking
description: Lower the other clips while this one plays, so music drops under a voice-over and comes back up after it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Ducking lowers the other clips while this one plays. The usual use is a voice-over: turn ducking on for the voice, and the music drops under it.

<AtAGlance where="Clip tab ▸ Sound ▸ Ducking" tools="set_audio" />

## Duck the music under a voice-over

Set ducking on the clip you want to hear, not on the clip that should get quieter.

<Steps>

1. Select the voice clip and open the **Sound** sub-tab of the Clip tab.

2. Open the **Ducking** section and tick **Duck other audio**.

3. Set **Level** to how loud the music should be under the voice.

</Steps>

Ticking the box starts from the defaults: down to 20 %, over 0.5 s, and back up over 1 s. Unticking it, or choosing **Reset** in the section's header, turns ducking off and forgets the settings. The header shows the level, such as "20%", or "off".

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Duck other audio** | Turns ducking on for this clip. | Off | |
| **Duck by** | What the ducking follows. See [Choose what it follows](#choose-what-it-follows). | Clip Length | Clip Length, Speech |
| **Level** | How loud the other clips are while this one plays. Quick picks: 0, 10, 20, 30 and 50 %. | 20 % | 0–100 % |
| **Attack** | How long the other clips take to fall to Level, starting from this clip's first frame. Quick picks: 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 s. | 0.5 s | 0–5 s |
| **Release** | How long they take to come back up, starting after this clip ends. Quick picks: 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 s. | 1 s | 0–5 s |
| **Pre-roll**, **Hold** | Only for Duck by Speech. See [Duck by Speech](/audio/duck-by-speech/#set-pre-roll-and-hold). | 0.5 s each | 0–5 s |

Every control but **Duck other audio** is greyed out until ducking is on. With several clips selected, changing one gives every selected clip all the first clip's ducking settings. See [Edit several clips at once](/audio/sound-tab/#edit-several-clips-at-once).

**Level** multiplies whatever the other clips are already doing, so at 20 % a clip at half volume plays at a tenth of its full level. Their own volume, fades and actions still apply underneath.

**Attack** and **Release** keep the length you type. They aren't rounded to whole frames. At 0 the level jumps instead of ramping.

## Choose what it follows

**Duck by** has two choices.

**Clip Length** keeps the others down for as long as the clip sits on the timeline, whether or not it's making a sound. They stay lowered through the pauses, so you can see exactly when ducking applies by looking at the timeline, and nothing extra is drawn on the clip.

---
title: Text clips
description: Add a title to the timeline, type its words, and see what else a text clip can do.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

A text clip puts words on the canvas: a title, a name strap, a line of explanation. It sits on a track like any other clip, and it has no source file behind it.

<AtAGlance
  keys="T"
  where={['The Add Text button in the timeline bar', 'Clip tab ▸ Text ▸ Content']}
  tools={['add_text_clip', 'set_text']}
/>

<Shot
  name="06-clip-text.window"
  alt="A title reading Frame Job selected in the preview, with an orange frame and handles around it. Its clip is outlined in the timeline, and the inspector's Clip tab is open on the Text sub-tab."
/>

## Add a text clip

Press <kbd>T</kbd>, or click **Add Text** in the timeline bar, the **Aa** button. There's no menu item for it.

The new clip reads "Title" in Source Sans 3 Bold at 72 px, in white, centred on the canvas, and it lasts 5 seconds. For a look sized to your canvas, use a [preset](/text-and-shapes/text-presets/).

It lands at the playhead on the front-most track if it fits there, and on a new track in front of everything if it doesn't. Either way it's one undo step, **Add Text**. With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open, the front-most track is the nest's own.

The clip comes in selected, so the canvas shows its handles and the **Clip** tab opens on its **Text** sub-tab. If the inspector is showing **Transcript** or **Assistant**, it stays there.

---
title: "Save, revert and close"
description: "Save a project as a .framejob package, let it autosave, make a copy, go back to an earlier version, and close it without losing work."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A project lives in a `.framejob` package. Save it once and Frame Job keeps the package up to date as you work, so most of these commands are about where the project lives and how to go back.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Save', 'File ▸ Duplicate', 'File ▸ Save As…', 'File ▸ Revert To ▸', 'File ▸ Rename…', 'File ▸ Move To…', 'File ▸ Share', 'File ▸ Close']}
  keys={['⌘S', '⇧⌘S', '⌥⇧⌘S', '⌘W']}
  tools={['save_project', 'close_project']}
/>

## Save a project

Press <kbd>⌘S</kbd> or choose **File ▸ Save**. An untitled project asks for a name and a place first. After that, a save writes straight to the package.

A project built around an opened movie, sound file or picture is untitled too. Its save panel opens in that file's folder with the file's name filled in, and the save writes a new package beside the file. It never writes over the file itself.

The window's subtitle tells you where you stand. It reads, for example, `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · edited` while there are changes that haven't been written, and the word `edited` goes when they have. It's the only sign of unsaved changes, and the close button shows no dot.

## Autosave

Once a project has been saved, it autosaves in place, the macOS way: your changes are written to the package as you work, and you don't need to press <kbd>⌘S</kbd>. A project that has never been saved has no package to write to, so save it first.

Because projects autosave, macOS adds its standard document commands to the **File** menu: **Duplicate**, **Rename…**, **Move To…**, **Revert To ▸** and **Share**.

## Crash-safe writes

Every save, autosaves included, writes the new package beside the old one and then swaps it in. A crash part-way through a save can't leave you with half a package.

## Make a copy

| Command | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **File ▸ Duplicate** | <kbd>⇧⌘S</kbd> | Opens a copy of the project as a new untitled project. The original stays open as it was. |
| **File ▸ Save As…** | <kbd>⌥⇧⌘S</kbd> | Writes the project to a new package, and the window carries on in it. Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> with the **File** menu open and **Duplicate** becomes **Save As…**. |

## Revert to an earlier version

**File ▸ Revert To ▸** goes back to the last saved version, or lets you browse earlier versions of the package. It has no key.

Going back throws away the changes made since that version. The playhead returns to the start, and the selection and the in/out range are cleared.

## Rename or move a project

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **File ▸ Rename…** | Renames the project's package. |
| **File ▸ Move To…** | Moves the project's package to another folder. |

Click the window's title for the same two controls.

Both act on the package alone. Footage the project points at stays where it is, unless you've copied it in with [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/).

## Share a project

**File ▸ Share** opens the macOS Share menu for the project.

:::note
A package doesn't hold your footage until you've run [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/). Without that, whoever receives it sees a project with missing media.
:::

## Close a project

Press <kbd>⌘W</kbd> or choose **File ▸ Close**. What happens depends on the project.

| The project is | What Close does |
| --- | --- |
| Saved | Writes any changes and closes without asking. |
| Untitled, with changes | Asks whether to save first. |
| Built around an opened movie, sound file or picture | Asks whether to save first, even if you've changed nothing. It always counts as an untitled project with changes. |
| Untitled, with no changes | Closes without asking. |

Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> with the **File** menu open and **Close** becomes **Close All** (<kbd>⌥⌘W</kbd>).

## A project saves only as a package

A project only ever saves as a `.framejob` package. **File ▸ Save** can't make a movie or a still. Those are separate steps: see [the export sheet](/export/export-sheet/). What a package holds is on [The .framejob package](/reference/framejob-package/).

## With an agent

- [`save_project`](/mcp/tools-projects/#save_project) finishes only once the package is on disk. It needs a path the first time, and passing a path later writes there, as **Save As…** does. There's no tool for **Duplicate**.
- `save_project` won't write to a path another open project holds, so close that project first. It won't write to a path a window is still opening either: call it again once the window has opened, or pass another path.
- [`get_project`](/mcp/tools-projects/#get_project) reports `unsaved_changes`, so an agent can see whether anything is still unwritten.
- [`close_project`](/mcp/tools-projects/#close_project) writes nothing. Where **Close** would save a project's changes, the tool leaves the project open unless you pass `discard`, which loses them. It also leaves a window open while a sheet is up. Once a project is closed, a call naming its path fails until the project is opened again.
- The [Assistant](/assistant/what-it-can-do/) asks you before it saves, and it can't close a project, because that would close the window its conversation lives in.

See [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/).

## Related

- [Undo and saving](/getting-started/undo-and-saving/)
- [Open a project](/projects/open-a-project/)
- [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/)
- [The .framejob package](/reference/framejob-package/)
---
title: "Consolidate Media"
description: "Copy every file a project uses into its package, so you can hand it over, move it or archive it without the originals."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A project normally points at your files where they are. Consolidate Media copies them all into the `.framejob` package and points the project at the copies, so the package becomes the whole edit. You can then hand it to someone, move it, or archive it and delete the originals.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Consolidate Media…"
  where="Media tab footer ▸ Consolidate…"
  tools="consolidate_media"
  needs="A saved project, and room on the disk for a second copy of the footage."
/>

## Consolidate a project

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Consolidate Media…**, or **Consolidate…** at the foot of the [Media tab](/projects/media-tab/). Both are off when the project has no media. If the project has never been saved, you'll [save it first](#save-the-project-first).

2. Watch the **Consolidating Media** sheet as the files copy.

3. Read what the sheet reports, then choose **Close**, or **Show in Finder** to see the copies.

</Steps>

Every file in the media list is copied into a `media` folder inside the package, whether a clip uses it or not. To keep the package smaller, [remove](/projects/remove-media/) what you don't need first. [Unused only](/projects/media-tab/#unused-only) shows you what that is.

## Save the project first

An untitled project has no package to copy into. On one, the command asks "Save this project first?" and offers **Save…** and **Cancel**. After the save it carries on where it left off. Cancelling the Save panel stops the command.

## While it copies

The sheet shows a bar, a line such as "Copying 4 files (2.1 GB) into the package…", and the name of the file being copied. When every file is already inside and only the project's links need correcting, the line reads "Relinking 2…".

**Cancel** stops between files, so the sheet shows "Stopping…" until the file in progress is done. What was copied stays copied and the project points at it, and the rest keep pointing at the originals. The project always opens. Run the command again to copy the rest.

## When it finishes

The sheet says what happened and offers **Show in Finder** and **Close**. **Show in Finder** shows the package's `media` folder and closes the sheet. The changes to the project are one undo step called **Consolidate Media**.

| The sheet says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Copied 4 files (2.1 GB) into the package." | How many files it copied, cursor files included. |
| "No files needed copying." | Nothing was copied. It also appears beside the lines below when no copy succeeded. |
| "Stopped before the rest." | You chose **Cancel**. |
---
title: "Relink missing media"
description: "Point a project back at files that have moved, one at a time or a whole folder at once, and see what a relink changes and keeps."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A project points at your files where they are, so moving or deleting one leaves its clips with nothing to show. Relinking tells Frame Job where the file is now, or gives it another file to use instead.

<AtAGlance
  where={['The Missing media sheet, when a project opens', 'Right-click a row on the Media tab ▸ Relink…']}
  tools={['relink_media', 'get_project']}
/>

## When a file goes missing

A project always opens, even with files gone. For each missing file:

- Its clips keep their place on the timeline and show a slate, with no sound.
- Its row on the [Media tab](/projects/media-tab/) wears a coral **missing** badge.
- An export still runs, and writes the slate and silence for those clips.

Frame Job remembers a file by more than its path, so one you've moved or renamed is often still found and never shows as missing.

## Relink from the Missing media sheet

When a project opens with files missing, the **Missing media** sheet comes up. It reads "The project opened without these files: their clips keep their place on the timeline and show a slate until the files are found." Each file is listed with its old path, and the footnote counts them ("3 files").

<Steps>
---
title: "The .framejob package"
description: "See what a saved project holds, which parts Frame Job can rebuild and which it can't, and what happens when you move or copy a package."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A Frame Job project is one `.framejob` package: a folder the Finder shows as one file. It holds your edit, its caches and, if you ask for them, copies of your footage.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Save', 'File ▸ Consolidate Media…']}
  keys="⌘S"
  tools={['save_project', 'consolidate_media']}
/>

## What a package is

| Inside | What it is | Can Frame Job rebuild it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`project.json`](#projectjson) | The edit itself | No. A package needs it to open. |
| [`cache/`](#cache) | Thumbnails, waveforms, analyses and renders | Yes, though [cloud transcripts](#transcripts-are-worth-keeping) cost money. |
| [`media/`](#media) | Copies of your footage, only after **Consolidate Media…** | No. It may be the only copy. |
| [`graphics/`](#graphics) | Graphic modules, fonts, images and kept versions, only once you add a graphic, font or image | No. |

To look inside, Control-click the package in the Finder and choose **Show Package Contents**.

A project only ever saves as a `.framejob` package. A movie or a still is a separate step: see [Export](/export/formats/) and [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).

A save writes the new package beside the old one and swaps it in, so a crash part-way through can't leave half a package.

:::caution
A save keeps only those four things. Any other file you put inside a package is dropped at the next save, autosaves included.
:::

## `project.json`

This is the edit itself: the canvas, media list, tracks, clips and markers. It's the only thing a package needs in order to open.

A project from any earlier version of Frame Job opens, and the next save writes it in the current format. A project from a newer build won't open, and the message asks you to update Frame Job. See [Open a project from another version](/projects/open-a-project/#open-a-project-from-another-version).

If `project.json` can't be read as text, the message says "*name* does not contain a readable project.json." See [When a project won't open](/projects/open-a-project/#when-a-project-wont-open).

## `cache/`

Everything here is something Frame Job can rebuild, so a package with a missing or damaged `cache/` still opens and redraws.

| Folder | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `thumbs/` | Filmstrip thumbnails |
| `peaks/` | Waveforms |
| `loudness/` | Loudness measurements |
| `speech/` | Voice detection |
| `sync/` | The analysis for [Synchronize Audio](/audio/synchronize-audio/) |
| `transcripts/` | [Transcripts from AssemblyAI](#transcripts-are-worth-keeping) |
| `device-transcripts/` | Words recognised on this Mac |
| `analysis/` | [On-device analysis](/projects/media-analysis/): shot changes, faces, people and salient regions, sound events, and the masks for **Remove Background** and **Text Behind Subject** |
| `reversed/` | [Reversed clips](/speed/reverse/) |
| `ramp-audio/` | Sound for [speed ramps](/speed/speed-ramps/) |
| `isolated/` | [Voice Isolation](/audio/voice-isolation/) renders |
| `voiced/` | [Voice effect](/audio/voice-effects/) renders |

The per-file caches build in the background after an open, an import or a relink, and the timeline fills in as they finish. At most two files' sound caches build at a time. A cache that already matches its file is never rebuilt. Analyses and renders are made when something asks for them.

Masks can make a package much larger, because they're kept for every frame: a minute of 1080p video's masks take about 62 MB.

### Transcripts are worth keeping

A transcript from AssemblyAI costs money to make again, so treat `cache/transcripts/` as worth keeping. Everything else in `cache/` rebuilds for nothing but time.

## `media/`

This folder exists only after [Consolidate Media…](/projects/consolidate-media/), and it holds copies of your footage. Unlike `cache/`, it may be the only copy, so don't delete it.

By default a project doesn't copy your footage. It remembers each file's path and a Finder bookmark, and reads the file from there. The package stays small but depends on the footage staying put. Consolidate Media is how a package comes to hold everything it needs.

## `graphics/`

This folder exists once you add a [graphic](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/), or a font or image for one. It holds the graphic modules, the small programs that draw each graphic, and these folders:

| Folder | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `fonts/` | [Fonts](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) the graphics use |
| `assets/` | [Images](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) the graphics use |
| `history/` | The last 10 [kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions) of each module, one folder per module |

## How a package travels

Moving, copying or consolidating a package keeps its caches. Until an untitled project is first saved, its caches live in a temporary folder, and the first save copies them in.

When you open a package, any media missing from its stored path is looked for in the package's own `media/` folder under the same name. That's what lets you move a consolidated package. A working link is never replaced this way.

A referenced file that has moved is often found again through its bookmark. If it isn't, see [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/).

To take a project to another Mac, run Consolidate Media first, so the footage goes with it.

## Related

- [Save, revert and close](/projects/save-and-revert/)
- [Open a project](/projects/open-a-project/)
- [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/)
- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)
- [Where Frame Job keeps its files](/reference/file-locations/)
---
title: "Import media"
description: "Bring movies, sound, pictures and LUTs into a project with Add Media… or a Finder drop, and find out why a file won't come in."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Importing puts a file in the project's Media tab, ready to place on the timeline. Frame Job reads the file from where it already is, so nothing is copied and the project stays small.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Add Media…"
  keys="⇧⌘I"
  where={['Media tab ▸ Add Media…', 'Drag from the Finder onto the Media tab']}
  tools={['import_media', 'add_media']}
/>

<Shot
  name="10b-media-tab.inspector"
  alt="The Media tab of the inspector, with the Add Media… button and its ⇧⌘I shortcut at the top of the list, and a count of the project's items beside them."
/>

## Add media

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Add Media…** (<kbd>⇧⌘I</kbd>), or **Add Media…** at the top of the Media tab.

2. Pick one or more files, and choose **Open**.

</Steps>

Frame Job checks every file, then adds the ones it can read to the [Media tab](/projects/media-tab/) together, as one undo step. The step is called **Add Media**, or **Add 3 Media Files** for three.

The files are in the Media tab, not on the timeline. [Place them](/editing/add-clips/) from there. Thumbnails and waveforms are built in the background, so they fill in a moment later.

Adding a file that's already in the list changes nothing. A file Frame Job can't read shows an alert naming it, and the rest are still added.

## Drop on the Media tab

Drag files from the Finder onto the Media tab to add them to this project. It works like **Add Media…**, with one difference: a drop has no list of allowed types, so Frame Job tries every file you drop. That's how a format the panels don't list gets in.

A Finder drop anywhere else on the window, such as the canvas or the timeline, doesn't add to this project. It opens the file as a new project of its own, as a drop on the Dock icon does. See [Open a project](/projects/open-a-project/).

## What each way takes

The **Add Media…** and **File ▸ Open…** panels only let you pick the types they list. To bring in anything else, drop it on the Media tab.

| Files | **Add Media…** | **File ▸ Open…**, or a drop on the window or the Dock | A drop on the Media tab |
---
title: Open a project
description: Open a saved .framejob project from the File menu, the Finder or a drop, and see what happens with older, newer, damaged or incomplete projects.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A project is a `.framejob` package: one item in the Finder that holds your edit. This page is about opening one you've saved. To turn a movie, sound file or picture into a new project, see [Start a project](/projects/start-a-project/).

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Open…', 'File ▸ Open Recent ▸', 'File ▸ Open Recent ▸ Clear Menu']}
  keys="⌘O"
  where={['Double-click in the Finder', 'Welcome window ▸ Open Video…', 'Welcome window ▸ Recent', 'A drop on the Dock icon or a window']}
  tools={['open_project', 'relink_media']}
/>

## Open a saved project

Choose **File ▸ Open…** (<kbd>⌘O</kbd>) and pick the package, or double-click it in the Finder. A double-click on a `.framejob` always opens it in Frame Job.

The open panel lists projects along with QuickTime, MPEG-4 and M4V files, other movies, and M4A, MP3, WAV, AIFF, PNG, JPEG and HEIC files. Everything but a project opens as a [fresh untitled project](/projects/start-a-project/).

A `.fjgraphic` isn't a project, and **File ▸ Open…** doesn't list one. See [Share a graphic](/graphics/share-a-graphic/).

## Open a recent project

**File ▸ Open Recent ▸** lists what you've opened lately. Choose one to reopen it. macOS fills the list, and **Clear Menu** at the foot of it empties it.

The [Welcome window](/projects/welcome-window/#reopen-a-recent-project) shows the five most recent from the same list.

## Drop files to open them

Drag from the Finder onto a project window, the Welcome window or the Dock icon. Each file opens as a document of its own:

- A `.framejob` package opens that project.
- A media file opens as a fresh untitled project built around it, so several files make several projects.

Only projects and the types **File ▸ Open…** lists are taken: MOV, MP4, M4V and other movies, M4A, MP3, WAV, AIFF, PNG, JPEG and HEIC. Anything else is ignored, with one exception: a `.fjgraphic` dropped on the Dock icon [goes to the Import Graphic sheet](/graphics/share-a-graphic/#open-from-the-fin

:::caution

---
title: "Split clips"
description: "Cut clips in two at the playhead, and see what each piece keeps of the footage, actions, word timings and graphics."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Split cuts a clip in two at the playhead, so you can trim, move or remove one piece without touching the other.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Split"
  keys="⌘T"
  where="The scissors button in the timeline bar"
  tools="split"
/>

## Split at the playhead

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the frame you want to cut on.

2. Select the clips to cut, or select nothing to cut everything under the playhead.

3. Press <kbd>⌘T</kbd>, choose **Clip ▸ Split**, or click the scissors button in the timeline bar.

</Steps>

| What's selected | What gets cut |
---
title: "Delete, Ripple Delete and Lift"
description: "Remove clips or a stretch of the timeline, and choose whether the hole stays open or closes up."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

---
title: Transitions
description: How a transition works in Frame Job, as the overlap between two clips on a track, and the rules that decide where one can go.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A transition carries the picture and sound from one clip into the next. In Frame Job it isn't a separate object you drop on a cut. It's what plays wherever two clips on the same track overlap.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Transition ▸"
  where="Clip tab ▸ Clip sub-tab ▸ Transition"
  tools={['add_transition', 'set_transition', 'set_transition_style', 'set_transition_duration']}
/>

## What a transition is

A transition plays across the overlap between two clips on the same track, and the overlap's length is the transition's duration. To make a transition longer, you make the overlap longer, by dragging or trimming a clip or by typing a [Duration](/motion/transition-settings/#duration).

The later clip carries the transition: it's the transition into that clip, and it's stored with that clip. To change one, select the clip that comes second.

There are thirteen [styles](/motion/transition-styles/), from Cross Dissolve to pushes, wipes and a zoom. [Add or remove a transition](/motion/add-a-transition/) has the ways to make one, and [The Transition section](/motion/transition-settings/) has its settings.

Two clips on different tracks don't transition, however they line up. They're layers, and the front one draws over the back one.

## Overlap two clips

The quickest transition is an overlap. When an edit leaves a clip overlapping the clip before it on the same track, and the later clip has no transition stored, Frame Job adds a Cross Dissolve. It's eased (**Ease In Out**) and crossfades the sound (**Crossfade Audio** on).

That holds however the overlap came about:

title: Corner radius
description: Round the corners of a video clip, image clip or freeze frame, from a soft edge to a pill or a circle.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Corner radius rounds the corners of a picture, which is handy for a picture-in-picture or a screen recording sitting on a background.

<AtAGlance where="Clip tab ▸ Picture ▸ Corner Radius ▸ Radius" tools="set_video" />

## Round the corners

<Steps>

1. Select a video clip, image clip or freeze frame and open the [Picture tab](/canvas/picture-tab/).

2. Open the **Corner Radius** section.

3. Drag **Radius**, type a value, or click the chevron for a [quick pick](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#use-a-quick-pick).

</Steps>

| Row | What it does | Default | Range | Quick picks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Radius** | How round the corners are, in source pixels | 0 px | 0 to 500 px | 0, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 |

Each change is one undo step. Closed, the section's summary reads the radius, such as `32 px`. **Reset** appears in its header while the radius isn't 0.

## How the radius is measured

The radius is in the source's own pixels, so it scales with the clip. A radius of 32 px on a clip at 50 % looks like 16 px on the canvas.

It rounds the [cropped](/canvas/crop/) picture, so the curve follows the crop rather than the original frame. A [shadow](/effects/shadow/) follows the rounded shape.

A radius can't be more than half the picture's shorter side, and anything above that draws as that half. So a big enough radius turns a wide picture into a pill and a square picture into a circle. **Radius** stops at 500 px, so it gets there only when the picture's shorter side, after any crop, is 1

## Animate the radius

With an [action](/motion/actions/) selected, **Radius** sets the action's end state, and the corners ramp there along the action's curve. See [Set what an action animates to](/motion/edit-an-action/).

## Good to know

Only video clips, image clips and freeze frames have this section. A rectangle shape has its own radius: see [Shape fill, stroke and size](/text-and-shapes/shape-settings/).

## With an agent

`set_video` sets this with `corner_radius`, in source pixels. It takes any value of 0 or more, without the inspector's 500 px stop. See [Tools: picture and grade](/mcp/tools-set-video/#crop-and-corners).

## Related

- [Shadow](/effects/shadow/)
- [The Picture tab](/canvas/picture-tab/)

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A camera layout decides how a camera clip and the screen recording behind it share the frame. Choose one at any moment and the picture eases into it there, so a tutorial can go from a small corner camera to a full-frame talking head and back as it plays.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Camera Layout ▸"
  where="Clip tab ▸ Picture ▸ Layout"
  tools="switch_layout"
/>

## Switch the layout

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to where the switch should start.

2. Tell Frame Job which clips to use. With nothing selected it looks for the track named "Camera", which is where a recording's camera lands, so usually there's nothing to do. Otherwise select the camera, or the camera and the screen. See [Which clips](#which-clips).

3. Choose a layout from **Clip ▸ Camera Layout ▸**.

</Steps>

To change layout again later, move the playhead on and choose another. To undo a switch, press <kbd>⌘Z</kbd>: one undo step, **Camera Layout**, takes the whole switch back. These items have no keyboard shortcut.

The [Layout section](/framing/layout-section/) in the inspector does the same thing for one selected clip, with a switch length you choose. To start a recording in a layout, [choose it in the recorder panel](/recording/camera-beside-the-screen/#choose-a-layout) before you record.

## The layouts

The submenu holds **Corner ▸**, **Rounded Corner ▸** and **Circle ▸**, each with **Bottom Right**, **Bottom Left**, **Top Right** and **Top Left**, then **Side by Side**, **Stacked**, **Camera Full** and **Screen Only**.

In the three corner layouts, Camera Full and Screen Only, the screen goes to its full placement. That's where **Add Clip** puts a new clip: centred, and scaled down to fit when it's bigger than the canvas and **Fit new clips to canvas** is on in the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/). A screen 

### Corner

The camera shows its whole picture, with square corners, in the corner you choose. It's fitted inside a box a quarter of the canvas wide and a third tall, 5 % in from the canvas's edges. This is the box a recording's camera lands in by default.

### Rounded Corner

The same box with rounded corners, the radius 8 % of the box's shorter side.

### Circle

The largest square of the camera's picture, cropped to a circle in the corner you choose. The circle is as wide as the box's shorter side, so on a 16:9 canvas it's a third of the canvas's height, and it sits 5 % in from the edges.

### Side by Side

The screen is fitted in the left two-thirds and the camera is cropped to fill the right third. There's a margin of 4 % of the canvas's shorter side around and between them, and both have their corners rounded by 2 % of that side. It needs a screen.

### Stacked

The screen runs across the top, centred, and takes up to two-thirds of the height inside the margins. The camera is cropped to fill the rest below it. The margins and corners are the same as Side by Side's. It needs a screen, and it works on any canvas, not only a tall one.

title: How sources are read
description: How Frame Job reads each kind of video and photo you bring in, and what it converts in an SDR project and in an HDR (HLG) project.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Frame Job reads each source as what it is: ordinary video, HLG video, an HDR10 file, wide-gamut footage or camera log. You don't need to set anything for most footage, because the file's own colour labels say how to read it. The one kind you may have to name yourself is camera log.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Add Media…', 'View ▸ Show Ungraded']}
  keys={['⇧⌘I', '⌃⌘U']}
  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log', 'Media tab ▸ HDR10']}
  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color']}
/>

## One conversion at the start

Each frame of a source is converted once, before anything else happens to it, into the colour the project works in. That's Rec. 709 in an SDR project and Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 in an HDR (HLG) project. See [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/) for how to choose.

The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture, so they work the same whatever the file was. The file's labels choose the conversion, and a [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) set on the file chooses before its labels. The conversion is Frame Job's own, for HLG, PQ and wide-gamut sources alike.

An SDR project that holds only Rec. 709 sources isn't converted at all. Its pixels and labels stay exactly as they are, because Frame Job turns the conversion on only when a source needs it.

A few terms come up below. A file's **primaries** say which colours its red, green and blue are, and its **transfer curve** says how its numbers turn into brightness. Brightness is measured in cd/m². A highlight that's **rolled off** is eased down to the brightest level the picture can show, rather than cut off flat.

| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Rec. 709 or untagged](#rec-709-and-untagged-sources) | Drawn as it is | Lifted to HDR reference white, so it looks the same |
| [HLG video](#hlg-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
| [PQ or HDR10 video](#pq-and-hdr10-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak | Real HDR, up to 1,000 cd/m² |
| [Wide-gamut SDR](#wide-gamut-sdr) | Converted to Rec. 709 | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
| [Camera log](#camera-log) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |
| [HLG or PQ still](#hdr-stills) | Converted as a video of the same kind is | Drawn in its own colour, as HDR |
| [Gain-map photo](#gain-map-photos) | Its ordinary picture | Its HDR highlights |

## Rec. 709 and untagged sources

Ordinary Rec. 709 video, video with no colour labels, recordings and stills are drawn as they are in an SDR project.

In an HDR (HLG) project they're lifted to HDR reference white, the level ordinary white sits at: 203 cd/m², or 75 % of the HLG signal. They look the same as they do in SDR, and HDR highlights rise above them. Text, captions, shapes, graphics and the background colour are lifted the same way.

## HLG video

HLG video, such as iPhone HDR video, needs no setting. The file's own colour labels choose the conversion.

title: Export size
description: Export at the document's size, a standard size or one you type, and see how Frame Job fits the picture to it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The **Size** popup sets the width and height of the exported file, whatever the size of your canvas. The [readout](/export/export-sheet/#the-readout-line) under the controls shows the numbers the file will have.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Size"
  tools="export"
/>

## Choose a size

Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Size**. Each row prints its numbers, for example `1080p · 1920 × 1080`.

| Row | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| **GIF default** or **APNG default** | The format's cap, 480 × 270 or 960 × 540. Only on those two formats, where it's the default. |
| **Document size** | The canvas as it is. The default for every movie format. |
| **Document (even)** | Takes the place of **Document size** when the format needs [even dimensions](#odd-widths-and-heights) and the canvas has an odd edge. It's one pixel smaller on that edge. |
| **4K** | A short edge of 2160 pixels. |
| **1440p** | A short edge of 1440 pixels. |
| **1080p** | A short edge of 1080 pixels. |
| **720p** | A short edge of 720 pixels. |
| **Custom…** | The [width and height you type](#type-a-custom-size). |

The number in a row's name is the short edge. The long edge follows your canvas's shape, rounded to the nearest even number:

| Canvas | **1080p** | **4K** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1920 × 1080 | 1920 × 1080 | 3840 × 2160 |
| 1080 × 1920 (vertical) | 1080 × 1920 | 2160 × 3840 |
| 1080 × 1080 (square) | 1080 × 1080 | 2160 × 2160 |
| 3024 × 1964 | 1662 × 1080 | 3326 × 2160 |

Changing **Format** rebuilds the list and puts it back on that format's first row, so a size picked for a movie doesn't follow you into a GIF.

## Type a custom size

<Steps>

1. Choose **Custom…** in **Size**. The two fields on the row below become editable, holding the size that was chosen a moment before.

2. Type a width and a height, from 16 to 8192 pixels each.

3. Press <kbd>Tab</kbd>, or click the other field. The readout updates then, not on each keystroke. Choosing **Export…** does the same.

</Steps>

A number outside the range stays in the field, and **Export…** beeps until you fix it. With a field empty, **Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out and the readout says "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list."

## Sizes that repeat

A row with the same numbers as an earlier row is hidden, so one size shows once, under the name that says more. A 1920 × 1080 document shows **Document size** and no separate **1080p**.
---
title: Export quality
description: Set how many bits an export spends on its picture and sound, from Format default to the four tiers.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The **Quality** popup sets the data rate of the picture and the sound. A higher rate gives a better picture and a larger file.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Quality"
  tools="export"
/>

## Choose a quality

Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Quality**: **Format default**, **Low**, **Medium**, **High** or **Maximum**. Each tier's title shows the rate it would ask for at the size and frame rate now chosen, for example `High · 8.0 Mbps`.

Once you pick a tier, the footnote shows the rates too, for example `H264 · MP4 · 8.0 Mbps · 256 kbps audio`. With **Format default** it shows no rates.

## Format default

The default row. Frame Job works the rate out from the frame's size and rate:

| Format | At 1080p, 30 fps | Bits per pixel per frame |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H.264 | About 8.7 Mbps | 0.14 |
| HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit | About 4.4 Mbps | 0.07 |
| AV1, VP9 | A [cap](#rates-on-av1-and-vp9) of about 4.4 Mbps | 0.07 |

The rate rises in step with the frame's area and the frame rate, and it's held between 1 and 200 Mbps. So H.264 at 1080p is about 8.7 Mbps at 30 fps, a little above **High**, and about 17.4 Mbps at 60 fps, where **High** is 12.0 Mbps.

The sound is 192 kbps AAC, or 192 kbps Opus in the WebM formats.

## The four tiers

Each tier sets the rate from the frame's size, so a tier means the same picture quality at every size. These are the H.264 rates at 30 fps or less:

| Tier | Bits per pixel per frame | 720p | 1080p | 4K | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Low** | 0.064 | 1.8 Mbps | 4.0 Mbps | 15.9 Mbps | 128 kbps |
| **Medium** | 0.096 | 2.7 Mbps | 6.0 Mbps | 23.9 Mbps | 192 kbps |
| **High** | 0.129 | 3.6 Mbps | 8.0 Mbps | 32.1 Mbps | 256 kbps |
| **Maximum** | 0.193 | 5.3 Mbps | 12.0 Mbps | 48.0 Mbps | 320 kbps |

A [preset](/export/presets/) stores the tier, not the number, so "High" works out the right rate on any document.

## How the rate scales

title: "The Export Queue"
description: "Write exports behind the editor, one at a time, while you keep working, and follow, cancel or reveal each one from a single window."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The Export Queue writes the same file as **Export…** without making you wait for it. Jobs run one at a time behind the editor while you keep working.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Window ▸ Export Queue"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Add to Queue"
  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
/>

## Add to Queue

<Steps>

1. Set up the file in the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/).

2. Choose **Add to Queue**. It's available whenever **Export…** is.

3. Name the file in the save panel and choose **Save**. This is the same panel **Export…** opens.

</Steps>

The **Export Queue** window then opens on its own, with the job in it. Your settings are remembered as the last choice, as they are for **Export…**.

Opening the export sheet pauses playback whichever button you use, but after **Add to Queue** no progress sheet is in the way. You can start playback again and go on editing while the job runs.

## The Export Queue window

Choose **Window ▸ Export Queue** to open it at any time. It has no keyboard shortcut.

The window lists every queued, running and finished export. Jobs run one at a time, in the order they were added, unless a job has to [wait for memory](#the-encoder-memory-wait). Closing the window stops nothing. Open it again and the jobs are where they'd got to.

The line at the bottom counts the jobs, for example "1 exporting · 2 waiting · 3 finished". With nothing in the list, the window reads "Nothing queued. The Export card's Add to Queue button puts a confirmed export here instead of waiting for it, and they run one at a time while you keep editing."

The list isn't saved. It starts empty each time you open Frame Job.

## Rows and their states

Each row shows the file's name and where the job has got to.

| The row says | What it means | Button |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Waiting` | Queued behind the running job. | **Cancel** |
| `Waiting for memory: …` | An AV1 or VP9 job [waiting for memory](#the-encoder-memory-wait). | **Cancel** |
---
title: "Export progress and the report"
description: Follow an export as it writes, cancel it, read its finish report, and find out why one failed.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

After you choose **Export…** on the export sheet, Frame Job asks where to save, then writes the file behind a progress sheet. When it's done, the sheet tells you what the sound measured and what went wrong, if anything did.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="The Exporting sheet"
  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
/>

**Add to Queue** opens the same save panel, then writes the file behind the editor so you can keep working. See [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/).

## The save panel

The save panel suggests the project's name with the format's extension, such as `Board v1.2.mp4`. Its message says what's being written:

| Format | Message |
| --- | --- |
| A movie | "Export the timeline as a movie." |
| Animated GIF | "Export the timeline as an animated GIF." |
| Animated PNG | "Export the timeline as an animated APNG." |
| Audio only | "Export the timeline's audio." |

Cancelling the save panel writes nothing. The export sheet has already closed by then, and it keeps the choices you made for next time.

## The Exporting sheet

**Exporting** shows a progress bar, a percentage and a status line. The status line moves through these:

| Status line | What's happening |
| --- | --- |
| "Preparing “*name*”…" | Frame Job is getting everything ready, and may be waiting for something the file needs. |
| "Measuring loudness…" | The sound is being [measured](/export/loudness/#how-normalisation-works). Every export with sound does this, whether or not you chose a target. |
| "Writing “*name*”…" | The file is being written. |

These zoom the preview. To zoom the timeline, see [Zoom and scroll the timeline](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/).

## Pinch and scroll

Pinch on a trackpad over the preview, or scroll with <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> held, to step through the same four stops. The stops are separate steps, so a gesture has to build up a little before it takes the next on

## Panning

When the zoomed canvas is bigger than the pane, there are two ways to move it:

- Scroll over the preview.
- Hold <kbd>Space</kbd> and drag. If you've been working elsewhere, click the canvas first, or <kbd>Space</kbd> plays and pauses instead of panning.

You can only pan in a direction where the canvas overflows the pane, so you can't drag the canvas out of view. While the canvas fits, a plain scroll does nothing.

Moving between stops keeps your pan, pulled back if it no longer fits. Going back to **Fit** centres the canvas again.

## Space on the canvas

After you've clicked the canvas, <kbd>Space</kbd> still plays and pauses. Frame Job can't tell a tap from a pan until you let go, so playback starts or stops on the release rather than the press. If you panned while <kbd

## Good to know

- The stops count up from **Fit** in order, whatever size Fit happens to be. On a small canvas in a large pane, **50%** can be smaller than **Fit**.
- While the canvas fits, holding <kbd>Space</kbd> and dragging a clip moves the clip as usual, and playback toggles when you let go of <kbd>Space</kbd>.

## Related

- [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/)
Frame Job reads <kbd>⇧</kbd> at every step of the drag, so you can change your mind before you let go, and the dashed outline follows.

A zoom changes a clip's scale and position, never its angle. On a rotated clip, fit and fill both allow for the rotation, and the dashed outline shows the result.

## Zoom Back

Zoom Back pulls the clip back out after a zoom.

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead past the end of the zoom, to where the pull-back should start. After Zoom to Region the playhead is still at the zoom's start, and a new action there would overlap it.

2. Click the zoom-out magnifier in the action lane.

</Steps>

Frame Job adds a 1-second **Ease In Out** action at the playhead whose end state is the clip's own scale, x and y, the values it has outside any action, whatever earlier actions did. There's no rectangle to draw and no k

Like <kbd>Z</kbd>, it beeps when there's no clip it can work on. See [Which clip can be zoomed](#which-clip-can-be-zoomed).

## Which clip can be zoomed

<kbd>Z</kbd> and Zoom Back need exactly one selected clip that's in the picture at the playhead and isn't on a locked track. Otherwise they beep. So they won't work with several clips selected, with the playhead off the 

The action also has to fit. Frame Job won't add a zoom that would overlap another action on the clip or run past the clip's end. It beeps and gives the reason at the foot of the inspector. If you'd drawn a rectangle the 

## Leaving the mode

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd>, press <kbd>Z</kbd> again, or click the zoom-in magnifier again. The mode also closes by itself when the selection changes or the playhead leaves the clip, and turning on another canvas tool, such as

Once focus has left the canvas, for example after a click in the inspector, <kbd>Esc</kbd> no longer reaches the mode, and <kbd>Z</kbd> is the way out.

A rectangle under 6 canvas pixels wide or high, or a click with no drag, beeps and leaves the mode on so you can draw again.

## The scale limit

The zoom stops at 1,000%, the largest scale a layer can take. The rectangle stays centred even then, but it doesn't reach the size you asked for. On a 1920-wide canvas, for example, a rectangle narrower than 192 pixels o

## With a During preset

On a clip with a During [motion preset](/motion/during-presets/), a second hint appears under the first: "This clip has During motion — the zoom is solved without it". The zoom is worked out as if the preset weren't ther

The hint follows the clip, so it appears or goes if a During preset is added or cleared while the mode is on.

## Auto Zoom

To zoom a screen recording at every click at once, use **Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…**. It plans these same zoom actions from the recording's cursor file. See [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/).

## Good to know

- You draw on the picture as it is at the playhead, with earlier actions applied, so you can draw a tighter zoom on a clip that's already zoomed.
- The rotation and crop are read at the start of the zoom. If you then animate either of them in the same action, the rectangle drifts across the action's span.

## With an agent
