title: Limits
description: Every hard number in Frame Job in one place, from how many clips a project holds to each area's ceilings.
---

The hard numbers, in one place. Each section gives an area's ceilings and links to the page that explains them. For what to do when you hit one, see [Troubleshooting](/reference/troubleshooting/).

## Project size

| A project holds at most | |
| --- | --- |
| Clips | 4,096 |
| Tracks | 64 |
| Markers | 1,024 |
| Media files | 1,024 |
| Levels of nesting | 8 |

Clips and tracks inside [nests](/editing/nests/) count towards the same totals.

An edit that would go past one of these isn't made, and an alert names the limit, for example "too many clips: 4097 (max 4096)". A project file already past a limit won't open, the message names the l

A [recording](/recording/where-it-lands/) that needs a new track can't be added to a project at its track limit. Its files stay on disk and the note names them.

Files in a project have one more limit: a [`.cube` LUT](#colour) can be at most 32 MiB.

## Canvas and layers

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| [Canvas](/projects/canvas-size/) width and height | Even numbers, 16 to 16,384 px |

## Open a movie

Any of these does the same thing:

- Choose **File ▸ Open…** (<kbd>⌘O</kbd>), or **Open Video…** on the [Welcome window](/projects/welcome-window/), and pick the file.
- In the Finder, choose **Open With ▸ Frame Job**.
- Double-click the file, once you've made Frame Job the default app for that file type.
- [Drop the file](/projects/open-a-project/#drop-files-to-open-them) on the Dock icon or on a Frame Job window.

Frame Job appears under **Open With** for movies and for M4A, MP3, WAV, AIFF, PNG, JPEG and HEIC files, but it doesn't take over their double-click unless you make it the default.

You get an untitled project with the movie as its first media file and its first clip, at the very start of Track 1. The window is named after the file, so `Interview.mov` opens as "Interview".

A WebM or MKV file is [copied into a movie](/projects/webm-and-matroska/) first. A file macOS can't open may still come in [through ffmpeg](/projects/ffmpeg-conversion/), if you have it installed.

## Open a sound file

Open a sound file the same way. A sound file has no picture to take a size from, so its project is 1920 × 1080 at 30 fps, with the sound as the first clip on Track 1. A movie file that holds only sound gets the same project.

## Open a picture

Open a PNG, JPEG or HEIC the same way. The project takes the picture's pixel size, runs at 30 fps, and holds the picture as a 5-second clip on Track 1.

## The size and rate you get

| You open | Canvas size | Frame rate | First clip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A movie | The size it displays at | The file's exact rate | The whole movie |
| A sound file | 1920 × 1080 | 30 fps | The whole sound |
| A picture | Its pixel size | 30 fps | 5 seconds of the picture |

### Display size

A project built from a movie uses the size the movie displays at, after the file's rotation. A portrait phone clip opens as 1080 × 1920, not sideways.

An odd-sized movie keeps its size, even though a canvas size you type must be even. Once you change either canvas field, both sides have to be even. See [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/).

### Exact frame rate

The rate is read from the file and never rounded to a neighbour, so 29.97 stays 29.97 and 23.976 stays 23.976.

A file's rate is matched to a standard rate if it's within 0.01 fps of one: 23.976, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 48, 50, 59.94 or 60. Any other rate is kept to three decimals, so a 47.3 fps screen recording isn't called 48. A movie that reports no usable rate opens at 30 fps.

Every file you [add to a project](/projects/import-media/) is read the same way. To change the project's rate later, see [Project frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/).

## Start a blank project
/>

## What it shows

The picture keeps the canvas's shape, letterboxed to fit the pane to the left of the inspector. Under it, a small caption gives the canvas size and frame rate, for example `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps`.

The preview is also where you work on the picture: selecting clips, then moving, scaling, rotating and cropping them. That's covered in [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/), and zooming it in [Zoom and pan the preview](/canvas/zoom-and-pan/).

Two settings change how the preview is drawn, and neither touches an export:

- [Preview Quality](/timeline/preview-quality/) draws it smaller, so heavy projects play more smoothly.
- [The Preview Window](/timeline/preview-window/) shows the same picture in a second window, for another display.

## Preview tags

Small tags in the top-left corner of the pane tell you when the picture isn't the plain one. Each shows only while its **View** item is on.

| Tag | Means | View item |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ungraded** | The picture shows no clip's grade. | [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/) |
| **Selection** | The picture shows which pixels the selected adjustment clip's qualifier picks. | [Show Selection](/color/show-selection/) |
| **SDR Version** | The picture shows the project's SDR version. | [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/) |

<Shot
  name="04b-preview-scopes.preview"
  alt="The preview pane with the Ungraded tag in its top-left corner, the picture with its caption 960 × 540 · 30 fps underneath, and the scopes panel beside it showing a waveform over a vectorscope."
/>

The tags sit in that order, and a hidden tag leaves no space, so **Selection** moves into the corner when **Ungraded** is off. **SDR Version** shows in an SDR project too, where the picture doesn't change.

## Other View items

The **View** menu holds the other switches for the preview. Each has its own page.

| Item | Keys | What it does | Remembered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [**Safe Areas**](/canvas/safe-areas/) | | Shows the title-safe and action-safe guides, the same as the toolbar's **Safe** box. Checked when on. | Yes |
| [**Show Ungraded**](/color/show-ungraded/) | <kbd>⌃⌘U</kbd> | Shows the picture as if no clip were graded. | No |
| [**Show Selection**](/color/show-selection/) | | Shows what an adjustment clip's qualifier picks. It needs a selected adjustment clip to turn on. | No |
| [**Show SDR Version**](/hdr/show-sdr-version/) | | Shows an HDR project's SDR version. | No |
| [**Show Subjects**](/framing/show-subjects/) | | Draws the faces, people and salient regions found for the selected clip. | No |
| [**Scopes**](/color/scopes/) | <kbd>⌃⌘W</kbd> | Shows the scopes panel beside the picture. | No |
| [**Loudness Meter**](/audio/loudness-meter/) | <kbd>⌃⌘L</kbd> | Shows the live loudness column beside the picture. | No |

Remembered means between launches, for every project. The items that aren't remembered start off in each new window, as the [Preview Window](/timeline/preview-window/) does, and none of these changes an export.

**View ▸ Assistant** (<kbd>⌃⌘A</kbd>) sits nearby but doesn't change the picture. It opens the inspector's Assistant tab, beside the preview. See [Chat with the Assistant](/assistant/chat/).

## At the end

Playback stops at the end of the timeline, and the playhead stays there. Press <kbd>Home</kbd> to [go back to the start](/timeline/move-the-playhead/). With [Loop](/timeline/loop/) on, playback goes back to the start of the loop instead.

An empty timeline has nothing to play, so Play, <kbd>J</kbd> and <kbd>L</kbd> beep.

## After an edit

You can edit while the timeline plays. What you notice depends on what you changed.

### Look-only edits

A change that only alters how something looks, such as a clip's position, a colour or some text, redraws the frame in place. Playback isn't interrupted.

### Structural edits

A move, a trim, a new clip or anything else that changes the timeline's shape makes Frame Job rebuild what the preview plays, in the background. So does a change to the sound, such as volume, pan or the compressor. It keeps your place and keeps playing at the same speed. While you drag, the rebuild 

### Failed rebuild

If a rebuild fails, Frame Job shows the error and the previous version of the timeline keeps playing.

## Related
HLG video, such as iPhone HDR video, needs no setting. The file's own colour labels choose the conversion.

- **In an SDR project** it's converted to Rec. 709 with its highlights rolled off smoothly. A colour Rec. 709 can't show is eased toward its own brightness instead of being clipped.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it stays HLG, with its highlights above white intact. An HLG file over BT.2020 is used exactly as it is, and one over P3 or BT.709 primaries is converted into BT.2020.

In an SDR project, HLG is converted whatever its primaries. A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020.

## PQ and HDR10 video

A PQ file, usually called HDR10, is always converted.

- **In an SDR project** its highlights roll off to white at the peak read from the file. Colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness, as with HLG. You can override the peak in the Media tab's **HDR10** section. See [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/).
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it becomes real HDR, keeping its brightness up to 1,000 cd/m². If the file's peak is above that, its highlights are rolled off to fit. A peak of 1,000 cd/m² or less doesn't change the picture.

A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020, as with HLG.

## Wide-gamut SDR


1. Open the **Document** tab.

2. In the **Canvas** section, choose from the **Dynamic Range** popup.

</Steps>

| Item | What the project works in | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SDR** | Rec. 709 | Yes |
| **HDR (HLG)** | Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 | |

Switching is one undo step, **Dynamic Range**, and it changes no clip and no grade value. Choosing the item already showing changes nothing and makes no undo step.

The setting belongs to the whole project, so it works the same with a [nest](/editing/nests/) open. A new project starts as SDR.

## The Colour row

The **Document** section at the top of the tab shows your choice in its **Colour** row. It reads "SDR — Rec. 709" or "HDR — Rec. 2100 HLG".

## The HDR working space

An HDR (HLG) project composes every frame in HLG-encoded BT.2020, so HDR footage keeps its range all the way through to the file.

- An iPhone HDR clip keeps its highlights above white. HLG footage over BT.2020 passes through unchanged.
- PQ footage becomes real HDR, up to 1,000 cd/m². Brighter highlights are rolled off to fit, by the file's [peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/).
- Footage with a built-in [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) curve becomes real HDR.
- Frames are labelled BT.2100 HLG, and the 10-bit exports are tagged HLG.

In an SDR project the same HDR sources are converted to Rec. 709 instead, with their highlights rolled off. [How sources are read](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/) has the full table, HDR stills included.

## SDR material in an HDR project

SDR material is lifted so its white sits at HDR reference white, the level ordinary white sits at in HDR. It looks as it did, and HDR highlights rise above it.

That covers BT.709 or untagged video, stills and screen recordings. Wide-gamut SDR footage is converted into BT.2020 and lifted the same way.

White is fixed at 203 cd/m² (HLG 75 %). There's no setting for the reference white.

## Drawn layers

Everything Frame Job draws is drawn as it is in SDR, then lifted to HDR reference white. That means text, captions, burn-in timecode, shapes, SDR stills, graphics, and the background and shadow colours.

So a white title sits at reference white, not in the highlights, and a white graphic matches SDR white. Text, captions, shapes and graphics stay 8-bit even though they're lifted. See [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).

## Grades across a switch

Switching changes no grade value. The numbers stay as you set them, and the grade then runs on the project's working colour, with BT.2020's weights in an HDR (HLG) project.

A `.cube` look still reads its values as Rec. 709. In an HDR project the [Look section](/color/looks/) warns: "This project is HDR (HLG): a .cube LUT reads its values as Rec. 709."

content.content:
The camera fills the canvas, with square corners. It's scaled until no canvas shows, so a picture of another shape runs off two edges.

### Screen Only

The camera is hidden where it is, its opacity going to 0, and the screen goes to its full placement. The camera clip keeps playing, so its sound carries on.

## Which clips

Frame Job works out the camera and the screen from the selection and the playhead. They don't have to come from a recording: any clip with a picture can be the camera, and any clip with a picture behind it can be the screen.

| Selected | The camera | The screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two clips with a picture, on different tracks | The front one | The other one |
| One clip with a picture | That clip | The clip drawing behind it at the playhead |
| Nothing | The clip at the playhead on the front-most track named "Camera" | The clip drawing behind it at the playhead |

The clip drawing behind the camera is the front-most one playing at the playhead on a track behind the camera's. Frame Job passes over hidden tracks, [matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/), [adjustment clips](/color/adjustment-clips/) and clips with their picture switched off.

With no screen, the corner layouts, Camera Full and Screen Only lay out the camera alone. Side by Side and Stacked won't.

The items are dimmed when:

- the camera doesn't play at the playhead. A selected clip the playhead isn't on doesn't fall back to the "Camera" track
- three or more clips are selected, or two on one track
- a selected clip has no picture of its own, such as a text clip, an adjustment clip or a sound-only clip
- a sheet is open

The menu works inside an open [nest](/editing/nests/). There, the nest's canvas is the canvas and the "Camera" track is the one inside the nest.

## The switch

A switch eases from the old layout into the new one over 0.5 s from the playhead. It's a layout action on each clip, so you can see it on the clip's [action lane](/motion/action-lane/) and retime it like any other action. Each action sets position, scale, crop, corner radius and opacity.

- **At a clip's first frame** it cuts instead of easing. The layout becomes the clip's own placement there, and a one-frame action marks the cut. Each clip is judged on its own, so a camera that starts at the playhead cuts while the screen behind it eases.
- **Near an end** the switch is shortened to finish by the clip's end or the clip's next layout action, and it's never shorter than one frame.
- **While another layout is still easing,** the first one ends where the second begins.
- **Where a layout action already starts,** the new layout replaces it.

## How far a layout reaches

A layout holds until the next switch, so a camera cut into pieces stays in the corner.

Every later clip with a picture on the camera's track, and on the screen's, that starts before the next layout action on that track takes the layout as its own placement, with no easing. With no later switch, that runs to the end of the track. Each track's reach is worked out separately.

Those later clips keep their own actions, though an action that moves one can [stop the switch](/framing/layout-section/#a-layout-meets-a-zoom). Because a later clip takes the layout as its placement, removing the layout action afterwards doesn't put that clip back. Use Undo for that.

## When a switch is refused

A switch that can't be made changes nothing. Frame Job beeps, and [the foot of the inspector](/getting-started/refused-edits/#the-refusal-strip) shows the reason after "Refused:". The numbers in it are Frame Job's own ids for the clip and the action, and the timecode is when that clip starts or, in the first two rows, 

| The inspector says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "clip 12 does not play at 00:00:04:10" | The clip isn't under the playhead. Move the playhead onto it. With two clips selected, this can be the screen. |
| "no clip draws behind clip 12 at 00:00:04:10 to be the screen" | Side by Side or Stacked found no screen. Pick another layout, or put a clip behind the camera. |
| "clip 12 is a nest clip, which cannot draw a rounded corner or a circle." | A nest clip shows square corners only, so a nest can't take Rounded Corner or Circle as the camera. That goes for a later camera clip in the layout's reach too. Use Corner. |
| "The screen clip 8 at 00:00:00:00 zooms (action 10); nest the screen's clips…" | The clip holds a zoom or another moving action after the playhead. See [A layout meets a zoom](/framing/layout-section/#a-layout-meets-a-zoom), which also covers the sheet Frame Job usually offers here. |
| "action 10 on clip 8 already runs from …, and two actions on one clip may not overlap" | Two actions on one clip can't overlap, and the switch's span runs into another action, such as a volume change. Move the playhead, shorten the switch in the [Layout section](/framing/layout-section/), or move that action. |

## Good to know

- A layout sets position, scale, crop, corner radius and opacity on both clips, replacing what you'd set by hand. Rotation and everything else stay as they were.
- A nest clip in Side by Side or Stacked keeps square corners.
- Side by Side stays side by side on a tall canvas if you choose it there. [Make Vertical Version](/framing/vertical-what-changes/) is what re-lays your switches for a new shape, and it turns Side by Side into Stacked on a canvas taller than wide.
- The camera's crop in Circle, Side by Side and Stacked can [centre on the person](/framing/layout-section/#the-crop-centred-on-the-person) instead of the picture.

## With an agent

[`switch_layout`](/mcp/tools-framing/#switch_layout) does what the menu does, at any time rather than the playhead. An agent can also:

- name the camera and the screen itself. The screen must be on a track behind the camera's, and each must have a picture and play at that time
These are the choices of [Follow Subject](/framing/follow-subject/), plus **Speaker**. The two commands share one remembered choice, saved when you choose **Make**. It starts on **Subject**. If you last chose **Speaker**, Follow Subject, which doesn't offer it

### Zoom

How tight the frame is, from 100 to 400 %, in whole numbers. 100 % is the smallest scale at which a picture covers the new canvas. Higher values frame closer.

**Zoom** starts at 100 % each time you choose the command and isn't remembered. The one exception is the sheet that [comes back after a Speaker analysis](/framing/follow-speaker/#the-sheet-comes-back-after-analysis), which keeps what you set. The summary updat

### Where Empty

What a followed clip shows while there's nothing to follow.

| Choice | What the frame shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Show Whole** | The whole picture on a blurred copy of itself. This is the default. |
| **Center** | The middle of the picture. |

It's dimmed while **Follow** is **Center**. It's the same remembered choice as Follow Subject's.

### Make a copy

Ticked, the vertical version opens as a new untitled project and this project doesn't change. The copy is named after this project with the shape, such as "Interview (9:16)", "Interview (4:5)" or "Interview (1:1)". It carries the project's caches and analysis.

Unticked, this project itself becomes the vertical version.

The box is ticked each time you choose the command, and your choice isn't remembered. Only the sheet that comes back after a Speaker analysis keeps what you chose.

## Read the summary

Under the controls, the sheet says what **Make** will do, and it changes as you change a control. It opens with the new size, "Makes a 1080 × 1920 version.", and goes on with whichever of these apply:

| The summary says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Follows 3 clips." | Every clip that's followed, so it includes the clips the next two rows count. |
| "Follows the cursor in 2 clips, their own zooms and pans replaced." | Screen recordings that follow the pointer. |
| "Follows whoever is talking in 1 clip." | Wide shots framed on the speaker. |
| "Re-lays 2 camera layouts for the new canvas." | Camera layout switches made again. |
| "Shows 1 clip whole on a blurred copy." | Clips with nothing to follow at any point. |
| "Keeps 4 clips as placed." | Clips moved and scaled to the new canvas, not framed. |
| "Re-fills 1 background." | Blurred copies and background plates resized to cover the new canvas. |
| "Removes 1 blurred copy the framing replaces." | Old blurred copies that are no longer needed. |
| "Re-sizes 1 graphic to the new canvas." | Graphics exactly the old canvas's size. |
| "Updates 1 graphic module to the current template." | Older copies of a bundled template, in a copy only. |
| "Adds a Backgrounds track for the blurred copy." | A new track at the back for the blurred copies. |
| "Adds 1 more track behind it where clips overlap." | A further track, for copies that overlap in time. |
| "2 actions re-eased at a cut." | A shot change landed inside actions a clip already had, so each was split there and eased again on either side. |
| "2 actions carry a framing move." | A framing move couldn't fit between a clip's own actions, so those actions carry it. |
| "Re-lays 1 caption track for the new canvas." | Word captions paged again for the narrow frame. |

After those come single lines for what needs your attention:

- One line per camera layout switch: "Re-laid: Side by Side → Stacked at 00:00:10:00."
- One line per clip that isn't followed, or is only partly followed, with the reason: "Clip 6 is not followed: its media file is missing, so it is kept as placed." or "Clip 2 is followed, but it is shown whole on a blurred copy where no subject is found."
- One line per caption track that's kept as it was, and one per graphic module left as it is.

If the movies have already been analysed, the summary reads "Reading the analysis…" for a moment, and **Make** is dimmed until it's done.

If Frame Job can't make the new version, the summary says why and **Make** stays dimmed. When an analysis has to run first, Frame Job beeps after it instead and says why at the foot of the inspector. A project at its limit of 64 tracks, nests included, is one

## Get captions in and out

Three commands sit next to each other in the **File** menu. None of them has a keyboard shortcut.

| Command | What it does |
</Steps>

## The Loudness popup

The target is the integrated loudness of the whole mix: one figure for the file from start to end, in LUFS, measured to ITU-R BS.1770-4.

| Choice | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| **Off** | No normalisation. The export still goes through the master limiter, measures its sound and reports it. |
| **−14 LUFS (streaming)** | Where the main streaming services normalise. |
| **−16 LUFS** | The usual target for stereo podcasts. |
| **−23 LUFS (broadcast)** | EBU R 128 broadcast delivery. |
| **Custom…** | Any target you type in the field beside the popup, from −70 to 0 LUFS, to one decimal place. |

The popup works on every format with sound, ProRes included. It's greyed out for Animated GIF and Animated PNG, which have no sound.

With **Custom…**, the field starts from the target you had chosen, or −14 after **Off**. While it's empty, the sheet says "Type a loudness target in LUFS, or pick one from the list." and **Export…** is greyed out.

The sheet remembers your choice with the rest of your last export, and a [preset](/export/presets/) stores it.

## How normalisation works

The export measures the real mix first, then applies **one gain** to everything. Levels inside the timeline keep their relationship to each other, so a quiet line stays quieter than a loud one.

The progress line reads "Measuring loudness…" during this pass. It fills the first tenth of the progress bar on a movie export, and the first half on an audio-only one.

The gain is worked out through the master limiter, so the file lands on the target even when its loudest peaks would pass the ceiling. Those peaks are turned down, not the whole mix.

The gain can be at most +40 dB, so a target more than 40 dB above the mix lands quieter than you asked. It's rounded to 0.01 dB, so two exports of one project get the same gain.

## What's kept

| What happened | Does the recording go on? | What lands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [A camera on its own stops](#a-camera-stops) | No | What was captured |
| [A camera beside the screen stops](#a-camera-stops) | Yes | The screen, and the camera up to the stop |
| [The microphone stops](#a-microphone-stops) | Yes | The picture, and the microphone's file only if [it can be used](#a-microphone-stops) |

| [The display sleeps or goes away](#the-display-sleeps-or-the-system-stops-the-recording) | No | What was captured |
| [A stretch's movie won't read](#a-stretch-wont-read) | It has already ended | Every other stretch, and that stretch's voice if it reads |
| [A file is too short for a frame](#a-file-is-too-short-for-one-frame) | It has already ended | That file in the Media tab, and the rest as usual |
| [The recording can't be added](#the-recording-cant-be-added) | It has already ended | Nothing, but the files stay on disk |

It can also read "its session was interrupted", or give a reason from macOS.

## Switch at Playhead

<Steps>

1. Select the camera clip, and only that clip. It needs to be a clip of a video file with a picture. An image, a still or a nest gets no Layout section, though [the menu](/framing/camera-layouts/#which-clips) can lay one out.

2. Open **Layout** in the Clip tab's **Picture** sub-tab. It comes after Transform and Behind Subject, and it's shut until you open it.

3. Set the [controls](#the-controls).

4. Move the playhead onto the clip, to where the switch should start.

5. Press **Switch at Playhead**.

</Steps>

This does exactly what **Clip ▸ Camera Layout ▸** does, with this clip as the camera and the clip drawing behind it as the screen. It's one undo step, **Camera Layout**. Everything in [The switch](/framing/camera-layouts/#the-switch) and [How far a layout reaches](/framing/camera

The button is off while a sheet is open. Pressed with the playhead off the clip, the foot of the inspector says the clip doesn't play there and nothing changes.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Choices |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Layout** | The layout to switch to. | Corner | Corner, Side by Side, Stacked, Camera Full, Screen Only |
| **Shape** | The corner picture's shape. Square is the menu's **Corner ▸**, Rounded its **Rounded Corner ▸**. Greyed for any layout but Corner. | Square | Square, Rounded, Circle |
| **Corner** | Which canvas corner the camera sits in. Greyed for any layout but Corner. | Bottom Right | Bottom Right, Bottom Left, Top Right, Top Left |
| **Duration** | How long the switch takes. | 0.5 s | 0.01 to 10 s |

The section's header sums up what it would switch to: "Square, Bottom Right", or "Side by Side".

Type a **Duration**, or pick 0.25, 0.5, 1 or 2 from the arrow in the field. A typed number outside the range goes to the nearest end of it. The switch is then rounded to whole frames, and a length under half a frame rounds to nothing, so Frame Job shows an error and doesn't switc

These choices belong to the section, not to the project. They stay while the window is open, they aren't saved and they aren't undo steps, so nothing changes until you press **Switch at Playhead**. There's no Reset.

## Grant Input Monitoring

Recording keys needs macOS's **Input Monitoring** permission. macOS shows no prompt for it, and Frame Job isn't in that pane's list until you add it, so pressing **Record** without the permission stops the recording from starting and opens System Settings for 

<Steps>

1. Press **Record**. System Settings opens at **Privacy & Security ▸ Input Monitoring**, and the panel's note says what to do.

2. Turn Frame Job on. If it isn't in the list, add it with **+**.

3. Back in the panel, press **Record** again. You don't need to relaunch.

</Steps>

Frame Job asks for this after Screen Recording, and before the camera and the microphone. See [Recording permissions](/recording/permissions/) for all of them, and for what changes if you started Frame Job from a terminal.

## What counts as a shortcut

A key press is a shortcut when you hold:

- <kbd>⌘</kbd> or <kbd>⌃</kbd> with any key.
- <kbd>⌥</kbd> with an arrow, Delete, Forward Delete, Return, Enter, Tab or Esc.

<kbd>⇧</kbd> on its own never makes a shortcut, and neither does <kbd>⌥</kbd> with any other key, because that types a character: <kbd>⌥E</kbd> starts an é.

A shortcut is stored with its keys spelled out, such as `cmd+shift+4`. The modifiers come first, in the order `cmd`, `ctrl`, `opt`, `shift`. The key comes last: a named key such as `return`, `tab`, `space`, `left` or `f5`, or otherwise the character the key ty

## Step frames

<kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> pause playback and move the playhead one frame. With <kbd>⇧</kbd>, they move ten. This is the way to place a cut exactly.

Stepping is silent, unlike a [scrub on the ruler](/timeline/ruler-and-playhead/#scrub-on-the-ruler). In the [Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-keys/), these keys move by word instead.

To go further in one press, see [Jump around the timeline](/timeline/move-the-playhead/).

## At the end
| --- | --- | --- |
| Play a clip at one new speed | [Clip ▸ Speed…](/speed/change-speed/) or **Rate** in the [Speed section](/speed/speed-section/) | The clip's start stays and its length changes. Later clips don't move
| Make a clip last an exact length | [Fit to](/speed/fit-to-duration/) | The rate changes so the clip plays in the length you type. |
| Stretch a clip by eye | [Rate stretch](/speed/rate-stretch/), <kbd>⌥</kbd>-dragging its end edge | The clip gets longer or shorter and still plays the same source. |
| Speed up and slow down inside a clip | A [speed ramp](/speed/speed-ramps/) | The clip keeps its place and length, and plays more or less of its file. |
| Speed up or slow down a stretch of the whole timeline | [Retime Range](/speed/retime-range/) | Every unlocked track changes together, and what follows moves up or back. |
| Speed up the typing in a screen recording | [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) | Only the stretches of typing change. |
| Play a clip backwards | [Reverse](/speed/reverse/) | Nothing on the timeline moves. |
| Hold one frame still | [Freeze Frame](/speed/freeze-frame/) | A still clip fills a gap opened at the playhead. |

A rate is a multiple of normal speed: ×1 is normal, ×2 is twice as fast and half as long, and ×0.5 is half speed.

Sound follows the [Keep pitch](/speed/keep-pitch/) setting, which is on for a new clip.

## Which clips take speed

Speed works on **media clips**, meaning clips of a video or audio file. Other clips have no source to speed up. Retime Range is the one exception.
9:Save Frame writes the frame under the playhead to a still image: a thumbnail, a poster frame or a picture for a document.
### Shape

Each row shows the size it makes, such as **9:16 (1080 × 1920)**. The new canvas keeps the old short side, rounded down to an even number, and the height follows from the shape.

| Shape | From 1920 × 1080 |
| --- | --- |
| **9:16** | 1080 × 1920 |
| **4:5** | 1080 × 1350 |
| **1:1** | 1080 × 1080 |

A shape the canvas already has isn't in the list.

### Follow

What each movie clip keeps in the frame.

| Choice | What the frame follows |
| --- | --- |
| **Subject** | A face. Where there's no face, a person. Where there's neither, the region the eye goes to. |
| **Faces** | Faces only. |
| **People** | People only. |
| **Salient Region** | Only the region the eye goes to. |
| **Speaker** | Whoever is talking, for a wide shot with a microphone per person. See [Follow the speaker in a vertical](/framing/follow-speaker/). |
| **Center** | The middle of the picture, for the whole clip. Needs no analysis, so the summary is ready at once. |

These are the choices of [Follow Subject](/framing/follow-subject/), plus **Speaker**. The two commands share one remembered choice, saved when you choose **Make**. It starts on **Subject**. If you last chose **Speaker**, Follow Subject, which doesn't offer it

## Good to know

- A filter covers the whole picture for the whole clip. To blur or pixelate one region, such as a face, use [Obscure](/effects/obscure/).
- With several clips selected, the rows show the first clip's stack, and any edit gives every selected clip that whole stack.
- A [nest](/editing/nests/) clip shows the Filters section, but a filter on it has no effect. Put filters on the clips inside the nest.
- On a [matte track](/canvas/matte-tracks/), a clip's filters shape the cut it makes. **Alpha** and **Inverted Alpha** read only transparency, so Sharpen, Sepia, Noir, Vignette and Invert change nothing there.
- A clip's [reflection](/effects/reflection/) shows its filters too.

92:- Add the overlays before you run [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/). It keeps each overlay on a Shortcuts track at normal speed.
104:- [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/)
## One kind of track for all sound

Frame Job has no separate audio tracks. Any track can hold a clip with sound:

- a video file
- an audio-only file, such as a voice-over, music or a recorder's take
- a microphone recording
- a clip split off with [Detach Audio](/audio/detach-and-attach/)
- a [nest](/editing/nests/) that holds sound

Each clip has its own processing on the [Sound tab](/audio/sound-tab/). Each track can be [muted or soloed](/audio/mute-and-solo/) and has its own [volume and pan](/audio/track-volume-and-pan/), [compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamic

The preview and the export use the same mix, so what you hear while editing is what gets written. There are two exceptions:

- The exported mix also passes through a master limiter the preview doesn't have, which holds its peaks under −1 dBTP unless an agent asks for another ceiling. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).
- A track's compressor and limiter are exact in an export and approximate in the preview. See [Track compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/).

## Drawing ahead while playing

While a preview plays forward over a project with a graphic in it, on the timeline or in a nest, Frame Job draws upcoming frames on spare processor cores ahead of the playhead. It uses one fewer core than your Mac has active.

It starts again from the new spot on play, on a seek, and on an edit while playing. It runs to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback is looping inside it.

It doesn't run while the preview is paused or playing in reverse. Background render covers paused.

## Kept frames

A window keeps the graphic frames it has drawn in memory while it's open, so a stretch you play again comes from memory rather than being drawn again.

A frame is matched by what it draws, so changing a module or a property only redraws the frames that come out different. Frames go when the window closes or newer frames replace them. The least recently used go first, and frames Background render drew ahead gi

## Background render

When you leave Frame Job alone, the window you last played or moved the playhead in draws its graphics ahead of the paused playhead, so the next play is smooth from the start.

| Setting | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Background render** | Turns background drawing on or off. | On | |
| **Start after … seconds** | How long Frame Job must be left alone first. | 5 | 1 to 60 |

Find them in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback**. They save the moment you change them, with no **Save** button, and they apply to every project. The ⓘ on the **Playback** heading explains them.

Background render needs a paused window that draws a graphic. It draws from the playhead to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback would loop inside it, and it ends early if the [memory budget](#the-memory-budget) runs ou

It keeps the processor busy while it runs, and it carries on while Frame Job is hidden or covered. It doesn't stop your Mac going to sleep. It only draws graphic frames, and it changes nothing in your project or your export.

## Set how long it waits

## Hidden and locked tracks

Clips on a hidden track aren't drawn, so you can't click them. A clip with its [picture turned off](/editing/enable-picture-and-sound/) draws nothing either, and can't be clicked.

Clips on a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/) are drawn, but you can't select or move them on the canvas. A click passes through to whatever is behind.

- A locked clip you select on the timeline shows its outline on the canvas, with no handles.
- If the front-most selected clip is locked, nothing gets handles, even when an unlocked clip is selected behind it.
- A drag of several clips leaves any on a locked track where they are.

## Good to know

- If the microphone stops on its own, for example because it's unplugged, the voice-over ends there. What was recorded lands, and the note reads "The microphone stopped recording on its own: … The voice-over ends where it stopped."
- A file too short to fill one frame stays in the [Media tab](/projects/media-tab/) without a clip, and a note says so. If that's every file, no **Microphone** track is added.
- A project already at its track limit can't take the new track. The files stay on disk and the note names them. See [Limits](/reference/limits/).

## Good to know

- An animated GIF or WebP shows its first frame only.
- A picture with transparency keeps it, so what's behind shows through.
- A picture more than 8,192 px on its long side is read at 8,192 px.
- Opening a PNG, JPEG or HEIC picture with **File ▸ Open…** builds a new project around it instead of adding it to the one you have open. See [Open a project](/projects/open-a-project/).

def main():
    failed = 0
    for rel, old, new in EDITS:
        path = ROOT / rel
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        count = text.count(old)
        if count != 1:
            failed += 1
            print(f"SKIPPED ({count} matches) {rel}: {old[:70]!r}")
            continue
        path.write_text(text.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"{len(EDITS) - failed} applied, {failed} skipped")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

app_defects.title: Dragging a clip past a holding action writes values you can't see
app_defects.evidence: Read from the code, not driven in the app. evaluate_clip in core/src/actions.rs merges every finished action's end state over the clip's base. A layout action names all six placement keys (core/src/action_class.rs). A recording's camera lands with a one-frame layout action at clip time 0 (core/src/edit_layout.rs, the t == 0 branch). CanvasEditTarget writes to the clip's base unless an action is selected. So after a recording lands with a camera, dragging or scaling the camera with the playhead past frame 0 changes the base and makes an undo step, but the picture doesn't change. The same applies past a zoom. The docs now give the workaround: select the action, step past it, then drag. The app could select the holding action itself, or say why nothing moved.

app_defects.title: Dragging a clip past a holding action writes values you can't see
app_defects.evidence: Read from the code, not driven in the app. evaluate_clip in core/src/actions.rs merges every finished action's end state over the clip's base. A layout action names all six placement keys (core/src/action_class.rs). A recording's camera lands with a one-frame layout action at clip time 0 (core/src/edit_layout.rs, the t == 0 branch). CanvasEditTarget writes to the clip's base unless an action is selected. So after a recording lands with a camera, dragging or scaling the camera with the playhead past frame 0 changes the base and makes an undo step, but the picture doesn't change. The same applies past a zoom. The docs now give the workaround: select the action, step past it, then drag. The app could select the holding action itself, or say why nothing moved.
